1	Cloud Access Security Broker (CASB)
     2	Given the increasing subscription to multiple clouds in many enterprises, one of the most
     3	important pieces of software is the cloud access security broker (CASB). It sits on the network
     4	between the cloud service customers (CSC) and the cloud service providers (CSP). The evolution
     5	of CASB functionality can be traced as follows [3]:
     6	• The primary function of the first generation of CASBs was the discovery of resources.
     7	They provided visibility into all of the cloud resources that the enterprise users accessed,
     8	thus preventing or minimizing the chances of shadow IT. Shadow IT is the practice of
     9	some users using cloud applications that are not authorized by the enterprise IT
    10	management from home or the office using enterprise desktops. An example of this is the
    11	use of unapproved software as-a-service (SaaS) applications for file sharing, social
    12	media, collaboration, and web conferencing [4]. This generation of CASBs also provides
    13	some statistics, such as software-as-a-service (SaaS) utilization.
    14	• The current generation of CASBs enforces security and governance policies for cloud
    15	applications, thus enabling enterprises to extend their on-premises policies to the cloud.
    16	Specific security services provided by CASBs include:
    17	o Protection of enterprise data that live in cloud service providers’ servers (due to
    18	SaaS or IaaS subscriptions), as well as data inflow and data outflow (i.e., Data
    19	Loss Prevention [DLP] capabilities) from those servers.
    20	o Tracking of threats, such as account hijacking and other malicious activities, some
    21	of which can detect anomalies in users’ cloud access behavior (through robust
    22	User and Entity Behavior Analytics (UEBA) functionality) and stop insider
    23	threats and advanced cyberattacks [5].
    24	o Detection of misconfigurations in the enterprise’s subscribed IaaS and cloud
    25	servers. These misconfigurations pose serious security risks, such as data
    26	breaches. Alerts generated by CASB due to misconfigurations in the enterprise’s
    27	IaaS deployments direct the enterprise to follow guidelines, such as the Center for
    28	Internet Security’s (CIS) benchmarks for public cloud services, thus improving
    29	the overall security profile of the enterprise for cloud access [4].
    30	Enhanced Firewall Capabilities
    31	The security functions in firewalls have enlarged alongside the changing network landscape.
    32	Firewalls started as hardware appliances that prevented network packets from a device with a
    33	particular network location (e.g., combination of Internet Protocol (IP) address and port) in one
    34	8
    35	NIST SP 800-215
    36	November 2022
    37	Guide to a Secure Enterprise
    38	Network Landscape
    39	subnet (e.g., external network or internet) from accessing a device on another network location
    40	or subnet (e.g., intranet or Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) or corporate network). In that setup, it
    41	primarily secured a network perimeter. The evolution of firewall functions can be traced based
    42	on the following feature sets [6]:
    43	• Packet filters and network address translation: Packet filtering and Network address
    44	translation (NAT) are used to monitor and control packets moving across a network
    45	interface, apply predetermined security rules, and obscure the internal network from the
    46	public internet.
    47	• Stateful inspection: Stateful firewalling, also known as dynamic packet filtering, monitors
    48	the state of connections and makes determinations as to what types of data packets belong
    49	to a known active connection and can be allowed to pass through the firewall.
    50	• Deep packet inspection (DPI): This feature, also known as packet sniffing, examines the
    51	content of packets (both the header and the payload, unlike the stateful inspection that
    52	inspects only the packet header). In addition to the capability provided by stateful
    53	inspection, this has capabilities related to finding hidden threats within the data stream,
    54	such as attempts at data exfiltration, violations of content policies, malware, and more.
    55	• Threat detection and response: Modern firewalls can gather and analyze enough data
    56	across multiple packets and sessions to detect threats and security incidents targeted at a
    57	particular system or a family of systems. These data from multiple firewalls can also be
    58	directed toward security information and event management (SIEM) and correlated with
    59	data from other security tools and IT systems to detect enterprise-wide attacks that span
    60	multiple systems and network layers. In addition, these data can be used to understand
    61	evolving threats and define new access rules, attack patterns, and defensive strategies [6].
    62	• Logging and auditing capabilities: Logging and auditing capabilities result in the
    63	construction of network events that can be used to identify patterns of performance and
    64	security issues.
    65	• Access control functions: Access control functions enforce granular sophisticated access
    66	control policies.
    67	• Multiple locations and functions: Firewalls reside at different locations to perform
    68	different functions. Firewalls at the network edge perform the network perimeter
    69	protection function by filtering disallowed sources and destinations and blocking the
    70	packets of potential threats. Firewalls inside a data center can segment the internal
    71	network to prevent the lateral movement of traffic and isolate sensitive resources (e.g.,
    72	services and data stores). Device-based firewalls prevent malicious traffic in and out of
    73	endpoints.
    74	• Open Application Programming Interfaces (APIs): These enable integration with many
    75	networking products that provide additional security capabilities.
    76	• Policy Composition Capabilities: Some firewalls can have the capabilities to merge
    77	policies at enforcement time so as to ensure that consistent policies are applied to
    78	different classes of users (e.g., those on-premises and on private and public clouds).
    79	• Web application firewalls (WAF): This class of firewalls has been used ever since web
    80	applications accessed through web protocols, such as Hypertext Transfer Protocol
    81	9
    82	NIST SP 800-215
    83	November 2022
    84	Guide to a Secure Enterprise
    85	Network Landscape
    86	(HTTP), came into existence. A feature advancement in this class of firewalls is
    87	advanced Uniform Resource Locator (URL) filtering. This is the ability to detect traffic
    88	from malicious URLs and prevent web-based threats and attacks by receiving real-time
    89	data analyzed by machine learning algorithms [7][8]. Specifically, this class of firewalls
    90	can inspect threat vectors for SQL Injection, operating system (OS) command injections,
    91	and cross-site scripting attacks, as well as prevent inbound attacks. They are used in
    92	content delivery networks (CDN) and to prevent distributed denial-of-service (DDoS)
    93	attacks. Some additional features found in this class of firewalls are:
    94	a. Ability to specify an allowable list of services (control at the application level)
    95	b. Traffic matches the intent of allowed ports
    96	c. Filtering of some unwanted protocols
    97	Appliance-set with Integrated Functions
    98	• Unified threat management (or UTMs): UTM devices combine many of the most critical
    99	security functions – firewall, IPS, VPN concentrator, gateway antivirus, content filtering,
   100	and WAN load balancing – into a single device, usually with a unified management
   101	console.

102	• Next-generation firewall (NGFW): The distinguishing feature of NGFW is application
   103	data awareness. It can look at data not only at layers 3 and 4 of an Open Systems
   104	Interconnection (OSI) stack but also at layer 7 – the application level. Its capabilities
   105	extend beyond packet filtering and stateful inspection. There are multiple deployment
   106	options available for NGFWs, such as an appliance in the data center, as a software
   107	running in a VM in a cloud, or as a cloud service (FWaaS). Some capabilities of NGFW
   108	include [9]:
   109	a. Deep Packet Inspection (DPI)
   110	b. TLS decryption and inspection of packet payload
   111	c. Intrusion prevention system (IPS) feature
   112	• Web application and API protection (WAAP): This is a comprehensive security approach
   113	and an enhancement over WAF. WAF is an integral component for API security, BOT
   114	(abbreviation for Robot) defense, and DDOS protection.
   115	a. These can be offered as a product suite or as a cloud-based service [10][11].
   116	b. Secure web gateway (SWGs): SWGs are appliances utilized for policy-based
   117	access to and control of cloud-based applications as well as governance of access
   118	to the open web for enterprise users in ubiquitous locations (e.g., headquarters,
   119	branch offices, home, remote locations). An SWG is fundamentally a web filter
   120	that protects outbound user traffic through HTTP or Hypertext Transfer Protocol
   121	Secure (HTTPS) inspection [12]. It also protects user endpoints from web-based
   122	threats that can occur when users click on links to malicious websites or to
   123	websites infected with malware. They centralize control, visibility, and reporting
   124	across many locations and types of users. They are not a replacement for WAFs,

   131	which protect websites housed in enterprise data centers and large headquarter
   132	sites from inbound attacks.

Based on `doc.txt` (NIST SP 800-215, "Guide to a Secure Enterprise Network Landscape"), the enhanced firewall capabilities described in the "Enhanced Firewall Capabilities" section benefit network security in the following ways:

- **Packet filtering and NAT**: Monitor and control packets crossing a network interface, apply predetermined security rules, and obscure the internal network from the public internet.
- **Stateful inspection**: Monitor the state of connections so only packets belonging to known active connections are allowed through.
- **Deep packet inspection (DPI)**: Examine both packet headers and payloads (unlike stateful inspection, which checks headers only), enabling detection of hidden threats in the data stream such as data exfiltration attempts, content policy violations, and malware.
- **Threat detection and response**: Gather and analyze data across multiple packets and sessions to detect threats and security incidents targeting a particular system or family of systems. Data from multiple firewalls can be fed to SIEM tools and correlated with other security tools to detect enterprise-wide attacks spanning multiple systems and network layers, and to understand evolving threats and define new access rules, attack patterns, and defensive strategies.
- **Logging and auditing**: Build a record of network events used to identify patterns of performance and security issues.
- **Access control functions**: Enforce granular, sophisticated access control policies.
- **Deployment at multiple locations**: Edge firewalls protect the network perimeter by filtering disallowed sources/destinations and blocking packets of potential threats; data-center firewalls segment the internal network to prevent lateral movement of traffic and isolate sensitive resources (e.g., services and data stores); device-based firewalls block malicious traffic in and out of endpoints.
- **Open APIs**: Enable integration with other networking products that add security capabilities.
- **Policy composition**: Merge policies at enforcement time so consistent policies are applied across different user classes (e.g., on-premises, private and public clouds).
- **Web application firewalls (WAF)**: Detect traffic from malicious URLs and prevent web-based threats using real-time machine-learning-analyzed data; inspect threat vectors such as SQL injection, OS command injection, and cross-site scripting; prevent inbound attacks; and are used in CDNs to prevent DDoS attacks. Additional features include specifying allowable service lists (application-level control), matching traffic to the intent of allowed ports, and filtering unwanted protocols.

In short, per the document, the evolution of firewall functions—from simple perimeter packet filtering to DPI, threat detection, granular access control, segmentation, and web application protection—broadens an enterprise's ability to detect, prevent, and respond to threats across the entire network, including enterprise-wide and web-based attacks.
